name: Ayurvedic amla / bhringraj / shikakai

card.summary: Traditional Ayurvedic hair herbs; centuries of use, no clinical hair trials.
card.aka: Indian gooseberry, Eclipta, false daisy, Acacia concinna
card.note: Traditional use; no high-quality clinical research on hair.

quick.overview:
Amla, bhringraj and shikakai are plants from the Ayurvedic tradition used as hair powders, pastes and oils. Amla is a vitamin C-rich fruit, bhringraj is Eclipta prostrata, and shikakai is a pod used as a mild cleanser.
Traditional users say they cleanse, condition and promote growth. Laboratory work exists on amla antioxidants, but no clinical hair trials were found.
quick.mechanism: Amla's tannins and vitamin C are the basis for antioxidant claims in laboratory studies. Shikakai-type plants are said to cleanse through natural saponins. Hair-growth mechanisms have not been shown in people.
quick.risks: No safety data exist for topical hair use. Wikipedia says no high-quality clinical research supports traditional uses of bhringraj.

lead: Amla, bhringraj and shikakai are three plant materials from the Ayurvedic tradition of South Asia that are used together or separately in hair care, as powders, pastes or infused oils. Amla is the fruit of Phyllanthus emblica (Indian gooseberry); bhringraj usually refers to Eclipta prostrata; shikakai is the pod, leaf and bark of the climbing shrub Senegalia rugata (formerly Acacia concinna), used as a mild natural cleanser [1][2][3].

People use them to look better through the hair: shikakai to cleanse without stripping natural oils, amla to condition and to add shine and perceived strength, and bhringraj, steeped in oil, to promote growth and darker hair. Wikipedia notes that Eclipta prostrata has been infused in coconut oil as a hair oil that was popular in Java until the 1970s, and that its leaves yield a black hair dye [2]. Shikakai has been used for hair on the Indian subcontinent since ancient times, and archaeobotanical traces of shikakai mixed with soap nuts and amla were found at the pre-Harappan site of Banawali, dated to about 2750-2500 BC [3].

Research on these herbs is largely laboratory work on amla's antioxidant properties and on plant constituents. Wikipedia states that no high-quality clinical research supports traditional uses of Eclipta prostrata [2]. A 2026 randomized trial of a polyherbal bhringraj hair oil (Neeli Bhringadi) in adults with androgenetic alopecia or greying reported improvements across measures of growth, density and greying, but it tested a multi-herb formula, with and without minoxidil, rather than the single herbs [12]. A 2025 systematic review of controlled trials of herbal hair-loss remedies covered rosemary, green tea, ginseng, aloe vera, olive and saw palmetto rather than these three herbs [13].

chain: Shikakai paste or powder cleanses hair with natural saponins
Amla and bhringraj are applied as pastes or oils to condition scalp and hair
Hair looks cleaner, shinier and, in users' accounts, thicker or darker
angle.text: Users wash with shikakai, condition with amla and oil the scalp with bhringraj, expecting softer, shinier, stronger-looking hair. Shikakai's cleansing action rests on saponins; the hair-growth and darkening claims for amla and bhringraj come mainly from tradition, with one randomized trial of a multi-herb bhringraj oil reported in 2026.

paras: Phyllanthus emblica is a deciduous tree, 1-8 m tall, native to tropical and southern Asia. Its greenish-yellow fruit is rich in ascorbic acid, and its bitterness is linked to ellagitannins such as emblicanin A and B, along with flavonoids, kaempferol, ellagic acid and gallic acid [1]. Ayurveda uses dried and fresh fruit as a common ingredient, including in the mixture triphala. The fruit is eaten raw, pickled with salt, oil and spices, added to dal or candied in syrup as murabba [1].

Hindi-speaking regions call Eclipta prostrata bhangra or bhringaraj, a name shared with the yellow-flowered Wedelia calendulacea. The plant is a daisy-family weed of warm, moist places worldwide, with synonyms including Eclipta alba [2]. In Southeast Asia the dried whole plant appears in traditional medicine. Javanese people infused it in coconut oil as a hair oil, and its leaves yield a black hair dye and are used in tattooing [2]. Its constituents include coumestans, polypeptides, polyacetylenes, steroids, triterpenes and flavonoids [2].

Shikakai is a spiny climbing shrub up to 5 m, native to Asia from India and Nepal through Southeast Asia and China. Its name comes from the Tamil for 'hair fruit' [4]. Dried pods, leaves and bark are ground into a powder and made into a paste. The shampoo lathers less than sulfate shampoos, has a naturally low pH, and is considered a good cleanser that does not strip natural oils; the bark is high in saponins, the foaming compounds responsible for cleansing [4]. Leaf infusions have been used in anti-dandruff preparations, and in Myanmar the fruit is combined with tayaw bark as a traditional shampoo used at New Year [4]. Soapnuts (Sapindus), a related saponin-containing cleanser, have pulp used to make soap and shampoo [3].

In the traditional routine described by practitioners, shikakai powder or paste is used as a cleanser in place of shampoo, amla powder or oil as a conditioning treatment, and bhringraj oil massaged into the scalp. Combinations of the three appear in commercial hair oils, herbal shampoos and hair powders in South Asia and in online natural-hair communities. Users report softer hair, reduced dandruff and slower greying. These are traditional and anecdotal reports. The pre-Harappan archaeobotanical find of shikakai, soap nuts and amla together points to long-standing use [4].

Shikakai has been used for hair on the Indian subcontinent since ancient times, and traces of shikakai mixed with soap nuts and amla were found at the pre-Harappan site of Banawali, dated to about 2750 to 2500 BC [4]. Eclipta prostrata was infused in coconut oil as a Javanese hair oil that stayed popular until about the 1970s, and its leaves yield a black hair dye [2]. The fruit of amla is a common ingredient in Ayurveda, including in the mixture triphala [1]. Taxonomically, a 2015 reassessment gave the name Senegalia rugata precedence over Acacia concinna for shikakai [4].

A 2016 review of amla covers its phytochemistry, ethnomedicinal uses and proposed molecular mechanisms [5], and an in vitro study compared antioxidant, anti-collagenase and anti-elastase activity of amla extract with other plant extracts for anti-ageing skin applications [6]. A 1999 paper examined the antioxidant activity of amla's tannoid principles, and later reviews describe its therapeutic potential and toxicology [7][8][9]. Eclipta alba has been studied in mice for pharmacokinetics of luteolin, wedelolactone and apigenin from an extract fraction [10], and a 2024 paper reported that bhringraj extract enhanced the sun protection factor of the sunscreen filter octocrylene in a lab formulation [11]. These are laboratory or review sources and do not test hair outcomes.

Wikipedia states that no high-quality clinical research shows medicinal uses of Eclipta prostrata to be effective [2]. Wikipedia's shikakai entry lists a safety assessment of Acacia concinna fruit extract among its references without summarising it, and notes that pod saponins have historically also been used to stun fish [4].

A randomized, double-blind trial published in Cureus in 2026 enrolled 78 adults aged 18 to 55 with androgenetic alopecia, hair fall or greying, of whom 75 completed it. Participants were assigned to Neeli Bhringadi polyherbal hair oil (a classical Ayurvedic oil used in scalp massage), the same oil plus 5% minoxidil, or 5% minoxidil alone, for 120 days [12]. Outcomes included growth rate, density, thickness, hair fall, scalp condition, anagen-to-telogen ratio, greying score and electron microscopy; all groups improved from baseline, and in the oil-only group the authors report growth rate rising to about 290 micrometres per day and density to about 278 hairs per square centimetre, with the oil described as well tolerated [12]. Several authors are affiliated with a contract research organisation and an Ayurvedic clinic, and the trial studied a multi-herb formula, so it does not isolate the effect of bhringraj, amla or shikakai individually [12].
No clinical trial of amla or shikakai alone for hair growth or hair quality in people was found. Laboratory research on amla antioxidant activity exists [6], but it does not address hair outcomes.
